title: Sourdough Garlic Knots Recipe: Shaping Tips with a Scraper
meta_description: Master the perfect sourdough garlic knots! Learn the best shaping techniques using a dough scraper for bakery-style results at home.
html:
There is something uniquely satisfying about the smell of garlic butter hitting hot, fresh sourdough. While a traditional sourdough loaf is a staple, turning that same fermented dough into bite-sized knots makes for an incredible appetizer or side dish. The key to a great knot isn't just the flavor—it's the structure and the way you handle the dough during the shaping process.

To get those professional, bakery-style swirls, you need the right technique and a few essential tools. This sourdough garlic knots recipe relies on a well-fed starter and a bit of patience, but the results are light, chewy, and deeply flavorful.

The Ingredients You'll Need

For the dough, you will need 500g of bread flour, 350g of warm water, 100g of active sourdough starter, and 10g of fine sea salt. For the garlic butter glaze, melt 1/2 cup of unsalted butter with four minced cloves of garlic, a pinch of salt, and fresh parsley.

When mixing your dough, I highly recommend using a Danish dough whisk. If you're just starting your sourdough journey, the 3-in-1 Sourdough Whisk Set (Whisk, Scraper, Lame) is a lifesaver. The Danish whisk is designed to cut through thick starters and heavy doughs without the batter getting stuck in the wires like it does with a standard balloon whisk.

Preparing the Sourdough Garlic Knots Recipe Dough

Combine your starter and water in a large bowl, then whisk in the flour and salt. Let the dough rest for 30 minutes (autolyse) before beginning your stretch-and-folds. Perform four sets of folds every 30 minutes to build strength. This ensures your knots hold their shape and don't flatten out in the oven.

After the bulk fermentation is complete—when the dough has grown by about 50% and feels airy—it is time to move to the counter. This is where your tool kit becomes essential. Using the dough scraper from the 3-in-1 Sourdough Whisk Set, gently turn the dough out onto a lightly floured surface. The scraper prevents the dough from sticking to your hands and keeps the gluten structure intact.

Shaping Tips: Using a Scraper for Precision

The secret to uniform knots is how you divide the dough. Instead of pulling at the dough with your fingers, which can tear the gluten, use your dough scraper to cut the mass into clean, equal-sized strips. For standard knots, aim for pieces about 2 inches wide and 6 inches long.

  1. Roll: Gently roll each strip into a thin rope, roughly 8 inches long. Avoid over-working the dough; you want to keep those fermentation bubbles.
  2. Twist: Twist the rope into a spiral, similar to how you would twist a piece of string.
  3. Knot: Tie the twisted rope into a simple overhand knot.
  4. Tuck: Use the edge of your dough scraper to gently press the end of the rope under the knot so it stays secure during the bake.

Using a scraper for the "tuck" phase ensures you aren't deflating the dough with your palms, resulting in a fluffier interior.

Baking to Golden Perfection

Place your knots on a parchment-lined baking sheet, leaving about an inch of space between them. Let them proof for another 30-60 minutes. While they proof, preheat your oven to 400°F. If you want a slightly crispier exterior, you can use a bread scoring lame from the 3-in-1 Sourdough Whisk Set to make a tiny, shallow slit across the top of each knot, though this is optional for this specific recipe.

Bake for 12-15 minutes until the knots are golden brown. The moment they come out of the oven, brush them generously with the melted garlic butter. The heat from the bread will pull the butter deep into the crumb, creating that signature savory finish.

Storing and Reheating Your Knots

Sourdough garlic knots are best eaten fresh, but they keep well for two days in an airtight container. To bring back the original texture, avoid the microwave, which can make sourdough rubbery. Instead, pop them in a 350°F oven or an air fryer for 2-3 minutes.

If you have extra dough, you can shape the knots and freeze them raw on a tray. Once frozen, transfer them to a freezer bag. When you're ready to eat, let them thaw in the fridge overnight and bake as usual.

FAQ

Why did my garlic knots turn out flat?

Flat knots are usually the result of under-developed gluten or over-proofing. Ensure you perform your stretch-and-folds during the bulk fermentation and avoid letting the shaped knots proof for too long before they hit the oven.

Can I use a regular whisk instead of a Danish dough whisk?

You can, but it is significantly harder. A standard whisk is too flimsy for heavy sourdough and often gets clogged with dough, making it difficult to incorporate the flour and starter evenly.

How do I stop the dough from sticking to the counter?

Use a combination of a light dusting of flour and a high-quality dough scraper. The scraper allows you to lift and move the dough without needing to add excessive flour, which can make the final knots too dense.
